question.text:
Which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)$ where $f(x)=\dfrac 1 8(x+4)(x+2)^2?$

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)
question.explanation:
The equation is already in factored form, so by the zero-product rule, we deduce that it has a single root at $x=-4$ and a double root at $x=-2.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

\begin{align*} y &= \dfrac 1 8(0+4)(0+2)^2 \\ &= \dfrac 1 8(4)(2)^2 \\ &= \dfrac 1 8 (4)(4)\\ &= 2 \end{align*}

So, the curve

  • intercepts the $y$-axis at the point $(0,2),$

  • passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=-4,$ and

  • touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=-2.$

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted ${\textsf{S}}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

question.text:
Given that $(x+2)$ is a factor of $f(x) = x^3 - 4x^2 - 3x + 18,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)
question.explanation:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x+2)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x+2)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+2)$ using synthetic division: \[ \begin{array}{c|rrrr} & x^3 & x^2 &x^1 & x^0 \\ {\color{red}{-2}} & 1 & -4 & -3 & 18 \\ & & -2 & 12 & -18 \\ \hline & 1 & -6 & 9 & 0 \end{array} \]

Therefore, \[ \dfrac{f(x)}{x+2} = x^2 - 6x + 9 \]

which means that \[ f(x) = (x+2)(x^2 - 6x + 9). \]

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get \[ f(x) = (x+2)(x-3)(x-3) = (x+2)(x-3)^2. \]

Now that we have the cubic in factored form, we can tell that it has a single root at $x = -2$ and a double root at $x = 3.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

\begin{align*} y &= (0+2)(0-3)^2 \\[3pt] &= (2)(-3)^2 \\[3pt] &= 18. \end{align*} So, the curve

  • intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,18),$

  • passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=-2,$ and

  • touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=3.$

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted ${\textsf{S}}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

Therefore, \[ \dfrac{f(x)}{x-1} = x^2 - 5x + 4 \]

  • intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,-4),$

  • passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=4,$ and

  • touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=1.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation: \begin{align*} y &=\dfrac{1}{3}(2-0)(3+0)^{2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{(2)(3)^2}{3} \\[5pt] &= 6 \end{align*}

So, the curve

  • intercepts the $y$-axis at the point $(0,6),$

  • touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=-3.$

Given that $x-4$ is a factor of $f(x)=-x^3 + 10 x^2 - 32 x + 32$, which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)
question.explanation:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x-4)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x-4)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-4)$ using synthetic division:

\[ \begin{array}{c|rrrr} & x^3 & x^2 &x^1 & x^0 \\ {\color{red}{4}} & -1 & 10 & -32 & 32 \\ & & -4 & 24 & -32 \\ \hline & -1 &6 & -8 & 0 \end{array} \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \dfrac{f(x)}{x-4} &= -x^2 + 6x - 8 \\[5pt] &= -(x^2-6x+8) \end{align*}

which means that

\[ f(x) = -(x-4)(x^2-6x+8). \]

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get \[ f(x) = -(x-4)(x-2)(x-4)=-(x-2)(x-4)^2 \]

Now that we have the cubic in factored form, we can tell that it has a single root at $x=2$ and a double root at $x=4.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation: \begin{align*} y &= -(0-2)(0-4)^2 \\[3pt] &= -(-2)(-4)^2 \\[3pt] &= 32. \end{align*}

So, the curve

  • intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,32),$

  • passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=2,$ and

  • touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=4.$

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the graph takes an ${\textsf{S}}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{f(x)}{x+2} & = -x^2 + x + 6 \end{align*}

which means that \begin{align} f(x) & = (x+2)(-x^2 + x + 6)\\[3pt] &= -(x+2)(x^2 - x - 6). \end{align}

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get \[ f(x) = -(x+2)(x+2)(x-3) =-(x-3)(x+2)^2. \]

Now that we have the cubic in factored form, we can tell that it has a single root at $x=3$ and a double root at $x=-2.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

\begin{align*} y &= -(0-3)(0+2)^2 \\[3pt] & = -(-3)(2)^2 \\[3pt] &= 12. \end{align*}

So, the curve

  • intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,12),$

  • passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=3,$ and

  • touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=-2.$
